headings.title: Introduction to Heartburn in Pregnancy
headings.content: Heartburn, or pyrosis, is one of the most common and uncomfortable gastrointestinal complaints experienced by women during pregnancy. Often described as a burning sensation rising from the epigastric region up toward the sternum and throat, it affects a significant percentage of expectant mothers, particularly as pregnancy progresses into the second and third trimesters. While heartburn is generally considered a benign and expected physiological consequence of carrying a pregnancy, its impact on the mother's daily comfort, nutritional intake, and overall quality of life should not be underestimated by nursing professionals. Expectant mothers frequently report sleep disturbances, anxiety regarding symptoms, and frustration with dietary limitations. For student nurses in Nigeria and globally, understanding heartburn in pregnancy is crucial for providing empathetic, evidence-based care. Nurses serve as the primary educators who can demystify these symptoms, reassure mothers that what they are experiencing is common, and intervene early with safe, non-pharmacological strategies before symptoms severely impact maternal well-being. Recognizing the physiological basis of this condition allows the nurse to establish a supportive therapeutic relationship, encouraging open communication about gastrointestinal discomforts during antenatal visits.

headings.title: Anatomy and Physiology of Pregnancy-Induced Acid Reflux
headings.content: The development of acid reflux during pregnancy is primarily driven by profound anatomical and hormonal changes that occur to support the growing fetus. Hormonally, the elevated levels of progesterone produced by the corpus luteum and later the placenta act as a potent smooth muscle relaxant. This systemic relaxation affects the lower esophageal sphincter (LES), the muscular valve responsible for preventing the backflow of acidic gastric contents into the esophagus. Because the LES tone is significantly reduced, gastric acid easily escapes upward. Anatomically, as the pregnancy progresses, the expanding uterus enlarges and exerts considerable mechanical pressure on the intra-abdominal organs. This physical crowding displaces the stomach upward and increases intra-gastric pressure, creating a high-pressure gradient that forces stomach contents through the relaxed LES. Furthermore, pregnancy slows down overall gastrointestinal motility due to progesterone-mediated smooth muscle relaxation, resulting in delayed gastric emptying. This prolonged transit time keeps food and acid in the stomach longer, increasing the likelihood of reflux episodes. For nursing students, grasping this dual hormonal and mechanical mechanism is essential for explaining to patients why heartburn occurs and why certain lifestyle modifications are necessary to counteract these physiological shifts.

headings.title: Etiology and Risk Factors
headings.content: While virtually every pregnant woman experiences some degree of hormonal influence on her gastrointestinal tract, several specific etiology factors and risk factors increase the frequency and severity of heartburn. Multiparity is a notable risk factor; women who have had previous pregnancies often experience earlier and more severe heartburn because their abdominal wall and supporting tissues have previously been stretched, allowing greater uterine displacement. A history of gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD) prior to conception strongly predisposes a woman to aggravated symptoms once pregnant, as her esophageal mucosa is already sensitive to acid exposure. Dietary habits also play a critical role in triggering episodes. Consuming large meals increases gastric volume and pressure against the LES. Additionally, certain foods and beverages are known to relax the LES or directly irritate the gastric mucosa, including citrus fruits, spicy dishes, tomato-based products, chocolate, peppermint, caffeine, and fatty or fried foods. Lying down immediately after eating removes the protective effect of gravity, facilitating reflux. Understanding these risk factors enables nurses to perform targeted risk assessments during antenatal booking and formulate individualized counseling plans that address modifiable triggers for each expectant mother.

headings.title: Clinical Manifestations and Subjective Assessment
headings.content: Clinical manifestations of heartburn in pregnancy are primarily subjective and reported by the patient during nursing assessments. The hallmark symptom is a retrosternal burning sensation that may radiate upward toward the neck, throat, or jaw, typically occurring shortly after eating or when bending over and lying flat. Patients frequently report an associated sour or bitter taste in the mouth, known as water brash or acid regurgitation, caused by the backward flow of gastric acid reaching the pharynx. Some women may experience excessive salivation, globus sensation (a feeling of a lump in the throat), or mild dysphagia due to esophageal irritation. Chronic irritation from acid exposure can also lead to a persistent dry cough, hoarseness of voice, or a sore throat, especially upon waking in the morning. During subjective assessment, nurses must actively listen to the patient's description of pain, noting the timing, duration, and aggravating or relieving factors. It is essential for nursing students to recognize that subjective complaints can vary widely in intensity from mild, occasional discomfort to severe, debilitating pain that interferes with adequate nutrition and sleep. A thorough nursing history establishes a baseline and helps guide appropriate interventions and referrals.

headings.title: Nursing Assessment and Differential Diagnosis
headings.content: Comprehensive nursing assessment involves gathering a detailed history of the patient's symptoms while remaining vigilant in performing differential diagnoses to rule out more serious medical conditions. While heartburn is benign, nurses must differentiate it from cardiac, biliary, and severe gastrointestinal pathologies that can present with similar epigastric or chest pain during pregnancy. For instance, myocardial ischemia or cardiac events, though less common in young pregnant women, must be considered if chest pain radiates to the jaw or left arm or is accompanied by shortness of breath and diaphoresis. Gallbladder disease, such as cholecystitis or biliary colic, can cause right upper quadrant pain that radiates to the back, often triggered by fatty foods. Peptic ulcer disease and severe preeclampsia (which can present with epigastric or right upper quadrant pain due to hepatic involvement) must also be ruled out. The nurse should assess vital signs, check blood pressure and urine protein to screen for hypertensive disorders of pregnancy, and evaluate pain characteristics. If "red flag" symptoms are present—such as persistent vomiting, hematemesis, melena, significant unintentional weight loss, or dysphagia—the nurse must immediately report these findings to the attending physician or midwife for advanced diagnostic evaluation, such as an endoscopy, ensuring patient safety.

headings.title: Non-Pharmacological Management and Lifestyle Modifications
headings.content: Non-pharmacological management and lifestyle modifications form the absolute first-line approach in treating heartburn during pregnancy, minimizing the need for medications and reducing fetal exposure to pharmacological agents. Nursing education should focus on practical, culturally adaptable lifestyle changes that the pregnant mother can easily incorporate into her daily routine. Dietary modifications include advising the patient to eat small, frequent meals (such as five or six mini-meals) rather than three large meals, which prevents gastric distension and reduces pressure on the lower esophageal sphincter. Patients should be instructed to eat slowly, chew food thoroughly, and avoid consuming large amounts of fluids with meals, which can over-distend the stomach. Specific trigger foods and beverages—including spicy, fatty, acidic foods, caffeine, chocolate, and carbonated drinks—should be identified and eliminated or minimized. Postural modifications are equally vital; mothers should be advised to remain upright for at least one to three hours after eating and to avoid bending over at the waist. Elevating the head of the bed by six to eight inches using blocks or wedge pillows helps use gravity to keep gastric acid down during sleep. Tight clothing around the abdomen should be avoided. Through supportive counseling, student nurses empower mothers to take an active role in managing their symptoms safely.

headings.title: Pharmacological Interventions and Safe Medications
headings.content: When lifestyle modifications and non-pharmacological interventions fail to provide adequate relief, pharmacological interventions may be introduced under medical supervision. The safety of the developing fetus is the primary consideration when selecting medications during pregnancy. Antacids are typically the first-line pharmaceutical option for rapid, short-term relief of acute heartburn. Antacids containing calcium carbonate, magnesium hydroxide, or aluminum hydroxide neutralize existing gastric acid effectively. However, nurses must caution patients against using sodium bicarbonate due to the risk of maternal and fetal fluid overload and metabolic alkalosis, and magnesium trisilicate is generally avoided for chronic use due to potential fetal toxicity. If antacids are insufficient, histamine-2 (H2) receptor antagonists, such as famotidine, may be prescribed, as they have a well-established safety profile in pregnancy and reduce acid production. Proton pump inhibitors (PPIs), such as omeprazole, are reserved for severe, refractory cases or diagnosed esophagitis and are prescribed after careful risk-benefit analysis by the primary healthcare provider. Nursing responsibilities include assessing the patient's medication history, educating on correct dosing, watching for side effects like constipation or diarrhea from antacids, and emphasizing that self-medication with over-the-counter remedies without consulting a midwife or physician should be avoided.

headings.title: Potential Complications and Patient Education
headings.content: Although heartburn is often viewed as a routine discomfort of pregnancy, unmanaged or severe chronic acid reflux can lead to potential complications that necessitate vigilant monitoring and thorough patient education. Chronic exposure of the esophageal mucosa to gastric acid can result in reflux esophagitis, characterized by severe inflammation, mucosal erosion, ulceration, and, in rare instances, stricture formation or Barrett's esophagus. Additionally, severe nocturnal heartburn significantly disrupts maternal sleep patterns, contributing to chronic fatigue, elevated stress levels, and emotional distress during pregnancy. Patient education delivered by nurses plays a pivotal role in preventing complications and promoting self-management. Nurses must educate expectant mothers on recognizing warning signs that require immediate clinical evaluation, such as persistent vomiting, hematemesis, black tarry stools, difficulty swallowing, or pain that radiates to the chest and arms. Education should also reinforce compliance with prescribed lifestyle changes, proper timing of meals, and the importance of consulting healthcare providers before taking any new herbal remedies or over-the-counter medications. By providing comprehensive and empathetic education, nursing students prepare mothers to navigate pregnancy with confidence and ensure both maternal and fetal safety.
